items.title: Psilocybin Report
items.content_html:
The United States has recently had a major renaissance in its understanding and acceptance of this little chemical called psilocybin. Psilocybin is the precursor of the active ingredient psilocin, which is shaped similarly to serotonin. It causes hallucinations and changes the fundamental structure of how different brain regions communicate with each other. Of course, it's colloquially known as magic mushrooms. And magic they are.

Psilocybin has been something I've been interested in for a long time. Almost serendipitously, after I moved to Colorado a few months ago, I realized that this state is only one of two (the other being Oregon) that has legalized psilocybin in therapeutic settings. Licensed clinicians supervise clients as they go through what's called the "journey." Because the effects of the chemical can be so intense and deeply moving, a lot of care must be taken in preparing properly for the journey and in the physical setting in which it takes place. Additionally, the clinicians screen for certain mental/physical disorders that would serve as contraindications to this experience. This is done to ensure you have the best possible chance at having a good journey.

The reason this chemical has been seeing increased attention over the years is that it's been shown to have clinically significant outcomes for people with certain disorders like Major Depressive Disorder, anxiety, PTSD, substance abuse, and many others. Psilocybin is currently going through a major clinical trial that is expected to convince the FDA to approve it nationwide as a legitimate form of treatment. As far as I know, I don't have any mental disorders, but regardless I felt it was going to help with some difficult life situations I was going through, as it seems to do for most people.

This post will chronicle my experience with the the 'shroom.

items.title: Pilgrimage
items.content_html:
It's not even the normal time of year for reflection on what has happened in the last twelve months, but these last four months have compressed within them what feels like a lifetime, so reflection seems unavoidable. I began this year with one measure of hope and another measure of deep dissatisfaction. I still had it in my head last January that life would go my way, that the plan I had devised for myself, for my small family of two, would unfold more or less accordingly.

Oh, how life likes to utterly fuck things up.

items.title: The Power of Now
items.content_html:
{ style="width: 100%; height: 300px; object-fit: cover; object-position: 0 30%" }

Five years ago, I first came to the mountains of the western United States. The trip was one of obligation, although an obligation I accepted willingly: the wedding of my girlfriend's (soon to be wife's) cousin and his bride. It sometimes happens that ordinary moments acquire extraordinary meaning only in retrospect. Looking back, I understand that this trip was never merely a story about attending a wedding or supporting my wife’s family.

It was the story of finding my home. And, in a way I would not understand until years later, it was the story of finding God.

items.title: Upheaval
items.content_html:
Far be it from me to be religious in the traditional sense. Those who know me know my embattled history with religion in my younger years. Still, I can't help but draw upon the ancient stories of the past to seek wisdom and parallels with the trials I face in life.

In the book of Exodus, the Israelites did not leave Egypt because they knew what came next. They left because they could no longer remain where they were. Generations of Israelites had lived in Egypt until a new Pharaoh came to see their growing population as a threat. He subjected them to forced labor, ordered increasingly brutal measures against them, and eventually commanded that their newborn sons be killed. Their suffering became so great that the story says their cries rose to God, who called Moses to lead them out of Egypt.

items.title: I Don't Know How I Got Here
items.content_html:
{ loading=lazy style="object-fit: cover;"}

One of my favorite life philosophies is something everyone has heard: it's better to ask for forgiveness than permission. I'm currently sitting outside by an alpine river in the San Juan mountains called Mineral Creek, which is situated downstream of two high alpine lakes called Ice Lake and Island Lake. I was forced to this spot not by choice, but because I had overstayed my welcome at my last campsite at the top of this place called Molas Pass. I knew I was over the 14 day limit, but I wasn't sure how strictly it was enforced. Apparently, very strictly. A Bureau of Land Management Police Officer knocked on my trailer door around noon, seemingly disappointed in me.

items.title: Out With Google Analytics, In With Cloudflare
items.content_html: Readers of my blog have unknowingly been contributing to something I shamefully admit: I've been tracking you. I know when you view my blog site, where you're from, what you're looking at, when you click on elements, and for how long you stay on my pages. This is made quite simple, actually. However, I realized my site tracking is no longer totally effective, and I found another easy way around it. This is how.
